title: Before Books Were Easy
summary: Long ago there were no books, no paper and no letters at all. People kept their stories in their heads and painted animals on cave walls. Then, in a busy city called Uruk, clever accountants began pressing little wedge marks into wet clay, and writing was born.

sections.heading: A World That Lived in Memory
paragraphs: Close your eyes and imagine a world with no writing at all. No books, no signs, no shopping lists, no birthday cards, no labels on cereal boxes. If you wanted to remember something important, such as which plants were safe to eat, where the river flooded, or who your great-great-grandmother was, you had exactly one place to keep it: inside your head. For almost all of the time that modern humans have existed, about 300,000 years, that was simply how life worked.

This does not mean people were forgetful or simple. In fact, people without writing often trained their memories to a level that would amaze us today. Knowledge was passed from older people to younger people by speaking, singing and showing. Historians call this oral tradition, from the Latin word for mouth. A grandmother might teach a child a long song that listed every family member back seven generations. A hunter might learn a story that was secretly a map, describing which hills, rocks and waterholes came one after another along a route.

We can still see how powerful oral tradition is in cultures that kept it alive. In West Africa, professional storytellers and musicians called griots have for centuries memorized the histories of kingdoms and families, performing them with music. The epic of Sundiata, about the founder of the Mali Empire in the 1200s, was carried for hundreds of years mainly by griots before scholars wrote it down. In Australia, Aboriginal peoples have songlines: long sung journeys that describe the land, its water sources and its sacred places, linking stories to the landscape itself.

The ancient Greek poems the Iliad and the Odyssey, said to be by Homer, were probably shaped by generations of singers who performed them aloud long before they were written down. In the 1930s an American scholar named Milman Parry studied singers in the Balkans who could perform poems thousands of lines long without any written text. He noticed that they used repeated phrases and patterns, like building blocks, to help them remember and improvise. The same kinds of repeated phrases appear in Homer, such as the famous 'rosy-fingered Dawn'.

Oral tradition had real strengths. It was free, it travelled wherever people travelled, and it could change to fit a new audience. But it also had weaknesses. If the only person who knew a story died suddenly, the story could vanish. Details could drift over time like a giant game of telephone. And there was one job that memory found especially hard: keeping track of lots of exact numbers. How many jars of oil did the temple receive last spring? How many sheep does a farmer owe? For questions like those, people needed something outside their heads. They needed marks.

sections.heading: Paint, Notches and Secret Signs
paragraphs: Long before anyone wrote a word, people were already storing information in pictures and marks. Some of the most breathtaking examples are hidden deep underground in the caves of Europe.

On 12 September 1940, an 18-year-old named Marcel Ravidat was exploring the hills near the village of Montignac in southwestern France. His dog, Robot, sniffed at a hole left where a tree had been uprooted. Ravidat came back with friends, squeezed down into the darkness, and found himself in a cave whose walls were covered with animals: horses, deer, wild cattle called aurochs, bison and even a mysterious creature that looks a bit like a unicorn. This was Lascaux, one of the most famous painted caves in the world.

Lascaux's paintings are usually dated to roughly 17,000 to 22,000 years ago, although scientists still debate the exact age. The cave holds around 6,000 figures in total, including more than 600 paintings and many hundreds of engravings scratched into the rock. Horses are the most common animal, with more than 360 of them. There is only one clear human figure, a strange stick-like man near a wounded bison, deep in a part of the cave called the Well.

The artists mixed their paints from natural minerals. Red and yellow came from iron-rich earth called ochre, and black came from charcoal or manganese. They blew paint through hollow bones, dabbed it with pads of fur or moss, and worked by the light of small stone lamps that burned animal fat. Some paintings are high up on the ceiling, which means the artists probably built wooden scaffolding.

Were these pictures a kind of writing? Not exactly. Nobody knows for sure what they meant. They may have been about hunting, religion, stories, seasons or something we cannot guess. But next to the animals, the artists also painted rows of dots, grids, lines and other repeated signs. Some researchers think these signs carried agreed meanings, perhaps counting days or marking events. That idea is still debated, but it shows that people were already experimenting with marks that stood for something.

Even older are tally marks: notches cut into bone or wood to keep count. The Lebombo bone, a baboon leg bone from the mountains between South Africa and Eswatini, carries a row of notches (often counted as 29) and is dated to roughly 42,000 to 43,000 years ago. The Ishango bone from what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, about 20,000 years old, has groups of notches that some people think show early arithmetic, though others say the patterns may be accidental. Tallies were simple but powerful: one notch, one thing.

Visitors loved Lascaux almost to death. After it opened to the public in 1948, the breath, body heat and moisture of more than a thousand visitors a day caused mould and damage, so the cave was closed in 1963. Today people visit careful copies instead, including Lascaux IV, which reproduces the whole cave and opened in 2016. It is a reminder that information stored on a surface can be fragile, a problem that will keep showing up all through the history of writing and printing.

sections.heading: Counting Goods in Uruk
paragraphs: Let us travel to a place where the story of writing truly begins: southern Mesopotamia, the flat land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in what is now Iraq. Around 5,000 years ago, a region called Sumer was home to some of the first true cities on Earth. The greatest of them was Uruk.

Imagine walking into Uruk around 3200 BCE. Mud-brick walls rise around you. Farmers lead donkeys loaded with barley along dusty streets. Canals shimmer with water carried from the river to the fields. On a raised platform stands a huge temple, the heart of the city, where priests and officials collect and store grain, oil, wool, beer and animals. Historians estimate that Uruk may have had tens of thousands of residents, making it one of the largest cities in the world at the time.

A city this big had a problem that no single memory could solve. Thousands of people were bringing goods in, taking rations out, paying what they owed and borrowing what they needed. Somebody had to keep accurate records. And the solution grew, step by step, out of something very humble: little pieces of clay.

For thousands of years before Uruk, people across the Near East had used small clay tokens to keep count. Archaeologists have found them at sites going back to roughly 8000 BCE, around the time farming began. The tokens came in different shapes: cones, spheres, discs, cylinders and little tetrahedrons. The archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat, who studied thousands of them, argued that each shape stood for a type of goods. A certain cone might mean a small measure of grain, a disc might mean a sheep. Three sheep would be three discs.

To keep tokens safe and honest, people sealed them inside hollow clay balls called envelopes, or bullae. Think of a clay piggy bank holding a receipt. If two people disagreed about a deal, they could break the envelope and count the tokens inside. But that destroyed the envelope. So people began pressing the tokens into the soft outside of the envelope before sealing them inside, leaving a picture of what was hidden within.

Then someone realised something brilliant: if the marks on the outside already showed the information, why bother with the tokens at all? A flat piece of clay with marks pressed into it could do the same job. According to Schmandt-Besserat's theory, this is how the first clay tablets with numbers and signs appeared. Not every scholar agrees with every step of her explanation, but nearly all agree on the big picture: writing in Mesopotamia grew out of accounting. The first writers were not poets. They were bookkeepers.

The earliest tablets from Uruk, from around 3300 to 3200 BCE, are mostly lists: so many measures of barley, so many workers, so many jars of beer. Archaeologists call this early stage proto-cuneiform. It used number signs plus little pictures for goods, such as a sheaf of grain or the head of an ox. It was not yet a way to write down spoken sentences. But it was the seed from which a full writing system would grow.

sections.heading: Wedges in Wet Clay: How Cuneiform Worked
paragraphs: Over the next few centuries, the simple counting marks of Uruk grew into a complete writing system. We call it cuneiform, from the Latin word cuneus, meaning wedge, because every sign is built from little wedge-shaped marks. It appeared in Uruk around 3300 to 3200 BCE and stayed in use for about 3,000 years, longer than the Latin alphabet has been used for English.

Here is how a scribe actually wrote. First, he (most scribes were men, though some women scribes are known) took a lump of fine, damp clay from the riverbank and shaped it in his palm into a tablet. Many tablets were small enough to hold in one hand, about the size of a phone or a bar of soap, though some were much larger. The clay had to be just right: wet enough to take a mark, but firm enough not to smear.

Next he picked up a stylus, a pen cut from a reed that grew along the rivers. The end of the stylus was trimmed to a sharp corner. Instead of dragging it across the clay like a pencil, the scribe pressed it in. Each press left a mark with a triangular head and a thin tail: a wedge. By turning the stylus to different angles and pressing harder or softer, he could make horizontal wedges, vertical wedges and slanting ones. Groups of wedges formed signs.

Pressing worked much better than drawing. Curved lines tend to drag up little ridges of clay, but quick straight presses stay clean and sharp. Over time the early picture-signs became more and more abstract, until the picture of an ox head no longer looked like an ox at all, just a neat cluster of wedges. This made writing faster. It also turned it into a code that had to be learned.

The biggest breakthrough was the idea of using signs for sounds, not just things. Scribes discovered the rebus principle, the same trick as drawing an eye and a saw to mean 'I saw'. A sign that meant one word could be borrowed for another word that sounded the same, or for one syllable of a longer word. With sound-signs, scribes could finally write names, grammar, and full spoken sentences. Early cuneiform used well over 1,000 different signs; later this was reduced to about 600 in common use, which was still a huge amount to memorise.

When the tablet was finished, it was usually left to dry in the hot Mesopotamian sun, which turned it hard like leather. Unfired tablets could be softened with water and reused, a little like a whiteboard. Important tablets that needed to last were sometimes baked in a kiln, turning them into something close to pottery. Some contracts were even sealed inside a clay envelope, with a copy of the text written on the outside, so nobody could secretly change the version inside.

Cuneiform turned out to be extremely adaptable. It was invented for the Sumerian language, but later peoples used it for Akkadian, Babylonian and Assyrian, and also for Elamite, Hittite, Hurrian and others, a bit like how the Latin alphabet is now used for English, Spanish, Vietnamese and Swahili. People wrote letters, laws, recipes, medical texts, school exercises, maths problems, star charts and epic poems on clay. One of the world's oldest great stories, the Epic of Gilgamesh, survives on clay tablets.

Learning cuneiform took years. Boys, mostly from well-off families, went to a school the Sumerians called the 'tablet house'. Teachers wrote a model text on one side of a tablet, and students copied it on the other side, over and over. Archaeologists have found thousands of these practice tablets, complete with mistakes. Some even record students grumbling about being punished by their teachers, a reminder that school has always been school.

Eventually, cheaper alphabets written with ink took over, and cuneiform faded away. The latest known cuneiform tablets, mostly astronomical records, date to around the first century CE. Then the script was forgotten for more than 1,500 years, until scholars in the 1800s, including Georg Friedrich Grotefend and Henry Rawlinson, worked out how to read it again.

sections.heading: Rolling Pictures: The Cylinder Seal
paragraphs: Now we come to an object that looks like a tiny rolling pin and contains one of the oldest seeds of the idea of printing. It is called a cylinder seal.

A cylinder seal is a small cylinder, often only a few centimetres long and about as thick as an adult's finger, carved from stone such as lapis lazuli, marble, obsidian or other hard rocks, and sometimes from shell or metal. Into its curved surface a skilled craftsman carved a design in reverse, cutting into the stone so the picture was sunk below the surface. This kind of carving is called intaglio. A hole was usually drilled through the middle so the seal could hang on a cord around the owner's neck or wrist, or be pinned to clothing.

To use it, you rolled the seal across a patch of soft, damp clay. Wherever the stone was carved away, clay pushed up into the hollows. The result was a raised picture, the right way round, that could be as long as you liked. Roll the seal once and you got the whole design. Roll it twice and the design repeated, like a pattern on wallpaper.

Cylinder seals were in common use in Mesopotamia by about 3500 BCE, around the same time the first cities and the first writing were developing, and they stayed in use there for about 3,000 years. Some scholars trace stamp seals and seal-like objects back even earlier. The designs could show gods, heroes fighting lions, rows of animals, banquets, and later the owner's name and title written in cuneiform.

Seals worked as signatures and as locks. A merchant might close a jar with a clay stopper and roll his seal across it. If the seal impression was broken, everyone would know someone had opened the jar. Doors of storerooms were tied shut with string, and lumps of sealed clay were pressed over the knot. On tablets, rolling a seal across the clay showed who had agreed to a sale, a loan or a marriage contract. Seals were so important that if someone lost one, they reported it to officials, so that anyone who used the stolen seal later could be caught out. People also believed seals could act as lucky charms that protected their owners.

Here is why the cylinder seal matters so much to our story. Think about what it actually does. A craftsman makes one carved original, in mirror image. Then that single original can create the same picture again and again and again, quickly and perfectly, on as many surfaces as you like. That is the central idea of printing: make a master once, then copy it many times. Mesopotamians were not printing books, and they did not use ink. But they were already using a reversed carved surface to reproduce an image, more than 4,000 years before Gutenberg.

sections.heading: Hieroglyphs and the Scribes of Egypt
paragraphs: While Sumerians were pressing wedges into clay, another great civilisation along the Nile River was developing its own writing. Egyptian hieroglyphs appeared around 3200 BCE. Some of the earliest known examples are small bone and ivory labels found in a royal tomb at Abydos in southern Egypt, dated to roughly that time. Whether the Egyptians got the idea of writing from Mesopotamia or invented it independently is still debated by historians, but their signs look completely different.

Hieroglyphs are beautiful little pictures: owls, feet, water ripples, reeds, snakes, hands, loaves of bread. The name comes from Greek words meaning 'sacred carvings', because the Greeks saw them on temples and tombs. But like cuneiform, hieroglyphs were not just pictures of things. Some signs stood for sounds, some for whole words, and some were silent helpers that showed what kind of word you were reading. By the Middle Kingdom, around 2000 BCE, the system used about 900 different signs, and in much later times the number grew into the thousands.

Carving hieroglyphs in stone was slow, so for everyday writing Egyptians developed faster, flowing forms. Hieratic was a joined-up script written with a brush. Much later, from around the 600s BCE, an even quicker script called demotic was used for business and legal papers. The beautiful carved hieroglyphs were kept for temples, monuments and tombs, a bit like the way we might use fancy lettering on a certificate but scribble a note in quick handwriting.

The people who could write all of this were called scribes, and they were rare and highly respected. Many historians estimate that only a small fraction of ancient Egyptians, perhaps around one percent, could read and write well, though such numbers are hard to know for sure. Becoming a scribe meant years of training, starting as a boy. Students practised by copying classic texts onto broken pieces of pottery and flakes of limestone called ostraca, which were free, before being trusted with more expensive materials.

A scribe's tool kit was simple but clever. He carried a long, flat palette, usually of wood, with hollows for two cakes of ink: black ink made from soot, and red ink made from ochre. Red was used for headings and important words, which is where the idea of a 'rubric' (from the Latin for red) in later books comes from. He wrote with a thin reed whose end was chewed or cut into a fine brush. A small pot of water let him wet the ink.

Being a scribe was a very good job. Scribes kept records of taxes and harvests, wrote letters for officials, copied religious texts and managed building projects. An old Egyptian text known as the Satire of the Trades, which students copied in school, tries to persuade boys to study hard by describing how tiring and dirty every other job is, from metalworking to fishing, and how comfortable life is for a scribe. Egyptians even believed writing was a gift from Thoth, the ibis-headed god of wisdom.

Hieroglyphs were used for well over 3,000 years. The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved in 394 CE at the temple of Philae. Afterwards, the knowledge was lost until the Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, carried the same decree in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek. Using it, the French scholar Jean-François Champollion announced in 1822 that he had cracked the code.

sections.heading: The Clay Library of Nineveh
paragraphs: To finish our first journey, let us visit one of the greatest libraries of the ancient world, built entirely of clay. In the 600s BCE, the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal ruled a vast empire from his capital city, Nineveh, near today's city of Mosul in northern Iraq. Unusually for a king of his time, Ashurbanipal boasted that he could read and write cuneiform himself.

Ashurbanipal wanted to own every important text he could find. He sent officials across his empire to collect and copy tablets on medicine, magic, astronomy, omens, prayers, history and literature. His scribes made fresh copies, often adding notes at the end about which original they had copied from and stating that the tablet belonged to the king. The result was a collection that today numbers more than 30,000 clay tablets and fragments. Many of them are actually everyday letters, reports and legal documents, but others are priceless works of literature, including the best-known version of the Epic of Gilgamesh.

Then disaster struck. In 612 BCE, armies of the Babylonians and Medes attacked and destroyed Nineveh. The palaces burned and collapsed. But here is the amazing twist: the fire that destroyed the city actually helped save the library. Many of the sun-dried tablets were baked hard in the flames, almost like pottery, which made them far tougher. Buried under rubble, they waited for more than 2,400 years.

In the middle of the 1800s, archaeologists including Austen Henry Layard and his assistant Hormuzd Rassam dug into the ruins of Nineveh and found huge piles of tablets in the palaces. Tens of thousands of them were shipped to the British Museum in London, where most of the collection is still kept. In 1872 a young British Museum worker named George Smith, studying one of the tablets, realised he was reading a flood story from the Epic of Gilgamesh that resembled the story of Noah. The news caused a sensation around the world.

Clay, then, had done an incredible job. It was cheap, it was everywhere, and when baked it could survive for thousands of years. Writing on it had let people keep accounts, make laws, send letters and save stories. And cylinder seals had shown that a single carved original could make copy after copy. But clay had serious drawbacks. A library of tablets weighed as much as a mountain of bricks. A long letter might need several heavy tablets. You could not roll it up and tuck it under your arm. And learning hundreds of complicated signs meant that only a small, highly trained group of scribes could read and write at all.
Clay was tough but heavy, so people began searching for lighter things to write on and simpler ways to write.

deepDive: Did writing appear once and spread, or was it invented several times? Most historians now think writing was invented independently at least three or four times: in Mesopotamia (around 3300 to 3200 BCE), in China (by about 1200 BCE, seen in oracle bone inscriptions from the Shang dynasty), and in Mesoamerica (by the first millennium BCE). Egypt is the tricky case. Its hieroglyphs appear around 3200 BCE, almost at the same moment as cuneiform, and the two regions were in contact, so some scholars argue the idea of writing travelled from Mesopotamia to Egypt, while others point out that the signs, materials and system look entirely Egyptian, suggesting an independent invention. The early Abydos labels have made the question harder, because they are roughly as old as the earliest Uruk tablets. The origin of cuneiform is also debated. Denise Schmandt-Besserat's token theory, published mainly in the 1970s to 1990s, is famous and widely taught: tokens, then envelopes with impressions, then tablets. Critics accept that tokens and envelopes existed, but question whether every token shape had a fixed meaning and whether the path to writing was really so direct, noting that many token types never became signs. What scholars largely agree on is that the earliest Mesopotamian writing was administrative. The large majority of the earliest Uruk tablets, often estimated at around 85 to 90 percent, are economic records, while literature appears centuries later. Another important idea is the difference between proto-writing and true writing. Tally marks, cave signs and token systems store information, but they cannot record any sentence of a spoken language. True writing arrives when signs systematically represent the sounds and words of a language, which in cuneiform happened through the rebus principle. Finally, it is worth noticing how much our knowledge depends on durable materials. Clay tablets survive in enormous numbers, so we know a lot about Mesopotamia, while writing on wood, leaves or cloth in other places may simply have rotted away, which can make some societies look less literate than they were.
funFact: The fire that destroyed the Assyrian city of Nineveh in 612 BCE accidentally baked many of King Ashurbanipal's clay tablets, helping thousands of them survive for more than 2,500 years.
